name: Mercurial
summary: A distributed version control system from the same month as Git, written mostly in Python, with a smaller command set, append-only storage and “phases” that stop you rewriting history others already have.
intro: Like Git, every Mercurial clone (`hg clone`) holds the full history, so commit, log, diff and merge run locally and `hg push` and `hg pull` exchange only what the other side lacks. Storage is different. Each file’s history is a revlog, which stores compressed deltas between revisions, with a full snapshot written whenever the deltas since the last one pass a threshold, so any revision is rebuilt from at most one snapshot and a short chain of deltas. Mercurial only ever appends to revlogs and never rewrites what it has written, which makes its transactions atomic: readers see a whole commit or none of it. A changeset points to a manifest (the list of files and their revisions), which points into each file’s revlog, and every entry is named by a cryptographic hash of its content.

Two features set its workflow apart. Phases record which changesets have been shared: new commits are `draft`, pushing them to a publishing server makes them `public`, and history-editing commands such as `rebase` refuse to touch public changesets, so you can’t accidentally rewrite what others have pulled; `secret` changesets are never pushed at all. And it has two kinds of branch: a named branch is stored in each commit and is permanent and global, while a bookmark is a movable label, closer to a Git branch. The separate evolve extension goes further, recording which changesets replaced which (obsolescence markers) so rewritten history can be shared safely.

Matt Mackall announced Mercurial in April 2005; it is licensed GPLv2 or later and is a member project of the Software Freedom Conservancy. The command-line tool `hg` is Python, with C and Rust for hot paths: optional Rust extensions speed up `status`, `commit`, `diff` and push and pull discovery, and `rhg` is an experimental pure-Rust front end that falls back for anything it doesn’t support. Several of its biggest users have moved on: Bitbucket dropped Mercurial in 2020, and Mozilla moved Firefox from Mercurial to Git in April 2025. The latest release is 7.2.4 (August 11, 2026).
strengths: Phases make history editing safe by default: `rebase` and friends refuse to rewrite changesets that are already public
Append-only revlogs with periodic snapshots keep any revision quick to rebuild and make interrupted writes harmless
A smaller, consistent command set and built-in help (`hg help`), with Python extensions to add commands
Scaled to very large monorepos: Facebook chose it over Git because its modular Python code was easier to extend
limits: A small ecosystem: Bitbucket removed Mercurial in 2020, and Python and Firefox have both moved to Git, so few hosts and tools support it
Named branches are written into every commit and can’t be deleted; short-lived work needs bookmarks instead
The Python implementation is slower than the experimental Rust `rhg` for the commands `rhg` supports, and `rhg` has to be built from source
Changeset evolution, the safe way to share rewritten history, still lives in a separate extension and is off by default

snippet.title: Clone, commit, and see phases and bookmarks
source: hg bookmark fix-greeting          # a movable label, like a Git branch
hg phase                          # draft: not shared yet, safe to rewrite
hg log -G -l 3                    # history as a graph, newest first
hg push -B fix-greeting           # share it; the changeset becomes public

story: In April 2005 the Linux kernel lost its free use of BitKeeper, and several people set out to write a replacement. Linus Torvalds started Git; Matt Mackall posted “Mercurial v0.1, a minimal scalable distributed SCM” to the kernel mailing list on April 19. His goals were to be as simple, and so as hackable, as possible, as scalable as possible, and efficient in memory, disk and bandwidth. The first version was under 600 lines of Python, and committing the 2.6.10 kernel took 27 seconds on his laptop. The kernel chose Git, but Mercurial found its own users.

Mercurial 1.0 shipped in March 2008, and projects such as Python and Mozilla’s Firefox ran on it for years. In January 2014 Facebook explained why it had picked Mercurial over Git for its huge monorepo: Git’s internals would be hard to change, while Mercurial was clean, modular Python. It added file-system watching and on-demand file fetching, and that extension work later grew into a separate system, Meta’s Sapling.

Then the field consolidated around Git and GitHub. CPython moved to GitHub in February 2017, partly because contributors already knew it. Bitbucket removed Mercurial support in 2020, saying under 1% of its new users chose it. Mozilla moved Firefox to Git on April 30, 2025. Mercurial itself keeps shipping: Python 3 only since 6.2 in 2022, more Rust in each release, and 7.2 in January 2026.

choices.why: Mackall’s first goal was to stay simple and hackable, so the core was a few hundred lines of Python, with C added later for hot paths. That is also why Facebook chose it: extensions could change almost anything without forking the tool.

Storing deltas saves space, but long delta chains make old revisions slow to rebuild. Writing a full snapshot whenever the deltas since the last one grow too large bounds the work, and only ever appending made writes safe to interrupt and friendly to `rsync` and HTTP range requests.

choices.choice: Track whether a changeset has been shared
choices.why: Rewriting history someone else has pulled creates duplicate changesets. Phases, added in Mercurial 2.1 (2012), mark changesets public once pushed, and history-editing commands refuse to modify them.

A named branch is stored in each commit, so the branch a change was made on stays part of its permanent, global record. For short-lived work Mercurial points to bookmarks instead: movable labels that advance with each commit and can be renamed or deleted without touching history.
